titleEn: Six-Year-Old With Severe Asthma Exacerbation - Pediatric Respiratory Distress

patient.name: Ava Thompson
patient.affectEn: sitting bolt upright on her mother's lap, leaning forward on her hands; anxious and tired but still interactive, clinging to her mother; pale; loud wheeze. If a stranger tries to force equipment on her, lay her down or take her off her mother's lap she pulls away and cries.
patient.speechEn: only 2-3 words at a time ("can't... breathe..."); her mother answers most history questions. After the first salbutamol course she manages 4-5 word phrases.

scene.settingEn: Tidy townhouse living room in Langley, 1930 hrs. Good lighting, no hazards. One patient: a 6-year-old girl sitting bolt upright on her mother's lap, leaning forward on her hands. Her mother is alone with her - frightened but cooperative. A used salbutamol MDI sits on the table. No fire response tonight; the nearest PCP car is 10 minutes out. Langley Memorial Hospital is 12 minutes away.
hazardsEn: infectious respiratory symptoms (two-day cold) - droplet precautions

bystanders.knowsEn: Asthma diagnosed at age 4. Two ER visits last winter, one of them an overnight admission - never intubated, never in ICU. A cold started two days ago; the wheeze began this afternoon and got worse tonight. She gave the salbutamol puffer twice this evening - two puffs each time, without a spacer - and it barely helped. Colds are her trigger. No pain - "she says it's hard to breathe, it doesn't hurt". Other history: eczema. Medications: salbutamol puffer as needed; fluticasone inhaler daily, "but we've been forgetting it lately". No known allergies - no food or drug allergies. A small dinner at 1800; drinking poorly today. Weight: about 21 kilos. She will hold a mask or the spacer for her daughter if asked, and wants to ride along in the ambulance.

scene.partnerEn: one partner at your licence level; acts only on your delegation
equipmentEn: pediatric and adult BVMs with masks
oxygen kit with pediatric masks (non-rebreather and simple) and tubing
salbutamol MDI (100 mcg per puff) with spacer and pediatric mask
PCP only: ipratropium (MDI and nebules), dexamethasone, epinephrine for IM injection, CPAP kit

dispatchEn: 1930 hrs. Code 3 to a townhouse in Langley. A 6-year-old girl with known asthma is having severe difficulty breathing. Her mother says she 'can barely talk'. Langley Memorial Hospital is 12 minutes away. No fire response tonight; the nearest PCP car is 10 minutes out.
dispatchUpdateEn: Dispatch adds: the child has had a cold for two days and her puffer "is not working tonight". She is conscious. Mother is alone with her.
arrivalEn: The mother opens the door of a tidy townhouse and leads you into the living room: "She can barely talk. Her puffer isn't working tonight." Good lighting, no hazards. One patient - her daughter, on her lap. A used salbutamol inhaler sits on the table.
firstLookEn: From the doorway: a small girl sitting bolt upright on her mother's lap, leaning forward on her hands. She looks anxious and tired but is watching you and clinging to her mother. You can hear her wheezing from the doorway; her nostrils flare and the skin between and below her ribs pulls in with every breath. She is pale, with no blue colour.

primary.locEn: Alert and interactive: clinging to her mother, watching you, answers in 2-3 words (AVPU = A). Anxious and tired.
primary.airwayEn: Patent. No stridor, no drooling, no barking cough. She can only get 2-3 words out between breaths.
primary.breathingEn: Rate 40, laboured: prolonged expiration with a diffuse expiratory wheeze in all fields on both sides, intercostal and subcostal retractions, nasal flaring.
primary.circulationEn: Radial pulse 132, strong, regular. Capillary refill 2 seconds. No bleeding.
primary.rbsEn: Rapid body survey (toe-to-head for her age): no hives or rash anywhere, no swelling of the lips or tongue, no injuries; dry eczema patches in the elbow creases. Skin pale, warm and dry, no cyanosis (skin is given automatically during the RBS).

history.ccEn: Child: "Can't... breathe..." Mother: "She's been wheezing since this afternoon, and tonight she can barely talk."

opqrst.oEn: Mother: "She's had a cold for two days. The wheeze started this afternoon and got worse tonight."
opqrst.pEn: Mother: "Nothing helps. I gave her puffer twice this evening - two puffs each time, without the spacer - and it barely did anything."
opqrst.qEn: Child: "Hard... to breathe." Mother: "It's the wheeze. She's working so hard."
opqrst.rEn: Mother: "She says it doesn't hurt anywhere."
opqrst.sEn: Mother: "She can only get two or three words out."
opqrst.tEn: Mother: "The cold started two days ago, the wheeze this afternoon, and it's been getting worse all evening."

history.painScoreEn: No pain. Child: "Doesn't... hurt." Mother: "She says it's hard to breathe, it doesn't hurt." (No numeric pain score applies.)

sample.sEn: Mother: "Wheezing, can't catch her breath, the cough and runny nose from her cold."
sample.aEn: Mother: "No allergies. No food or drug allergies."
sample.mEn: Mother: "Her salbutamol puffer when she needs it - I gave it twice tonight, two puffs each time, without the spacer. And a fluticasone inhaler every day, but we've been forgetting it lately."
sample.pEn: Mother: "Asthma since she was 4, and eczema. Two ER visits last winter - one time she stayed overnight. She's never needed a breathing tube and she's never been in ICU."
sample.lEn: Mother: "A small dinner at six. She's hardly drunk anything today."
sample.eEn: Mother: "She's had a cold for two days. The wheeze started this afternoon and tonight it got really bad. Colds always set her off."

fe.generalEn: Mother: "Just the cold for two days. Nothing else."
fe.respiratoryEn: Mother: "A cough and the wheeze since this afternoon. No high-pitched noise when she breathes in - not at any point."
fe.giGuEn: Mother: "She's hardly drinking today and she's been to the toilet less. No vomiting."
fe.integumentaryEn: Mother: "Just her eczema. No new rash."
fe.eentEn: Mother: "A runny nose. No ear pain, no sore throat."

findings.headNeckEn: Nasal flaring and a mild tracheal tug. No stridor, no drooling. Lips moist.
findings.chestLungsEn: Intercostal and subcostal retractions. Expiratory wheeze in all six auscultation sites, equal air entry, no crackles, no silent zones.
findings.abdomenEn: Soft, moving with respiration. No other findings.
findings.backEn: Posterior lung fields auscultated: wheeze throughout.
findings.lowerExtremitiesEn: No findings. No cyanosis, no clubbing.

vitalsSets.unlockNoteEn: on scene, done gently on her mother's lap, before salbutamol (baseline)

resp.character: prolonged expiration with diffuse expiratory wheeze

vitalsSets.unlockNoteEn: en route, about 7 minutes after set 1, after the first salbutamol course - improving; the pulse rise to 140 is the expected salbutamol effect

resp.character: wheeze still present, air entry improved; speaking 4-5 word phrases

stateChanges.examinerLineEn: She screams and pulls away, clinging to her mother. Her breathing is faster and even more laboured, and she can't get any words out.
She is getting tired. She has gone quiet, her eyes keep closing, and you can barely hear the wheeze any more.

resp.character: tiring; the wheeze is barely audible - a quiet chest

vitalsPatch.spo2: falling, lower than the last reading

expected.actionEn: Acknowledge and plan pediatric-sized equipment: pediatric BVM and masks, pediatric oxygen delivery, MDI spacer with a pediatric mask, and suction
Plan the pediatric approach in advance: assess from the doorway, keep the child on her mother's lap, get to her eye level, and never force interventions that will agitate her
triggers: keep her on her mother's lap

expected.actionEn: Anticipate a Rapid Transport Category call: a child in respiratory distress whose home salbutamol is failing
Verbalize hazards (none), environment, nature of illness (asthma exacerbation on top of a cold), people (one patient plus mother) and resources (PCP car en route)
Don gloves; use a mask given the child's infectious respiratory symptoms
Complete the Pediatric Assessment Triangle from the doorway and state the conclusion: abnormal work of breathing with a still-interactive child - respiratory distress, sick, move quickly
Assess LOC age-appropriately: alert, interactive with her mother - and recognize that agitation or drowsiness in this child would signal deterioration
Assess the airway and actively differentiate: no stridor, no drooling, no barking cough - lower airway bronchospasm, not croup or epiglottitis
Assess breathing fully: rate 40, prolonged expiration, diffuse expiratory wheeze on auscultation of both sides, retractions and nasal flaring - inadequate and worsening
Assess circulation: radial pulse 132 strong with capillary refill 2 seconds - perfusion still adequate
Rapid body survey done toe-to-head for a young child, specifically checking for hives, lip or tongue swelling to rule out anaphylaxis
Note the skin: pale, warm, dry, no cyanosis
High-flow oxygen for SpO2 89% with respiratory distress, delivered the least frightening way - mother holds the mask, or blow-by if the mask is refused; target SpO2 at or above 94%
Position of comfort: leave her sitting upright on her mother's lap - never force her supine and never separate her from her mother
Categorize as RTC out loud: pediatric respiratory distress with accessory muscle use and failing home salbutamol
Ready to load within 15 minutes, transported sitting up, with the remaining assessment done en route
triggers: rest of the assessment en route

expected.actionEn: Bring the mother in the ambulance: she is the child's consent-giver, historian, and the best tool for keeping the child calm
Establish the chief complaint: severe shortness of breath in a known asthmatic with a two-day cold
Take the HxC/C: onset and progression, what home treatment was given (doses, times, spacer or not) and its effect, plus the severity markers - prior admissions, ICU stays or intubations
Ask the child's weight - every pediatric drug dose depends on it
Past medical history
Medications, including tonight's salbutamol doses and adherence to the daily preventer
Allergies
Last oral intake, noting poor fluid intake today
GCS with all three components stated separately
Blood pressure with a pediatric cuff
Pulse rate, rhythm and quality - and note 132 as the pre-salbutamol baseline for later comparison
Respiratory rate, depth and character with both lung fields auscultated
Skin assessed hands-on
Pupils - size, equality and reaction
SpO2 monitored continuously, on and off oxygen values recorded
Temperature - indicated with two days of infectious symptoms
FE - General health
FE - CNS
FE - Respiratory (no stridor at any point keeps the diagnosis in the lower airway)
FE - Cardiovascular
FE - GI/GU (poor intake and fewer wet diapers or toilet trips flag dehydration in a child)
FE - Integumentary
FE - Musculoskeletal
FE - Endocrine
FE - EENT
Head and neck examined: work-of-breathing signs documented, airway red flags (stridor, drooling) rechecked
Chest auscultated at all six sites, listening specifically for silent zones - a quiet chest in asthma means worsening, not improvement
Abdomen examined
Back examined with posterior lung fields auscultated
Upper extremities with capillary refill
Lower extremities checked for cyanosis
Administer salbutamol by MDI with spacer and pediatric mask: 10 x 100 mcg for a 21 kg child, repeatable up to 3 times, with the 6 rights verbalized
Choose MDI with spacer over the nebulizer and say why: infectious respiratory symptoms make aerosol-generating nebulization the wrong first choice
triggers: MDI with spacer instead of a neb

expected.actionEn: Transport after the first course rather than staying on scene to finish all repeats
triggers: give the rest on the way
no need to stay for all three

expected.actionEn: Keep the BVM sized and within reach, and state the triggers for assisted ventilation: tiring, falling respiratory rate, decreasing LOC, or a silent chest
EMR: Verbalize what is outside EMR scope - ipratropium, dexamethasone, IM epinephrine, CPAP - and that CPAP is contraindicated at age 6 in any case
Keep the child calm throughout: interventions delivered on mother's lap, nothing forced
Reassess ABCs and interventions after each salbutamol course and at least every 5 minutes
triggers: recheck her breathing after the salbutamol

expected.actionEn: Second full set of vitals within 5-6 minutes, with the trend interpreted out loud as improving
Attribute the pulse rise from 132 to 140 to salbutamol rather than deterioration, and keep treating
State the deterioration triggers one more time: quiet child, silent chest, falling rate or LOC means BVM ventilation now
En-route notification to the receiving hospital for a pediatric respiratory patient
Complete verbal hand-off: severity history, treatment times and doses, and response to salbutamol
Accurate PCR completed within 5 minutes, weight documented

specialEvents.descriptionEn: candidate gives the salbutamol by nebulizer (aerosol-generating) despite her infectious respiratory symptoms, or by MDI without a spacer and pediatric mask

candidate gives a dose other than the sheet dose for this 21 kg child: a salbutamol MDI course other than 10 x 100 mcg (e.g. 4 or 5 puffs) or a nebulized dose other than 5 mg; PCP: ipratropium other than 80 mcg MDI or 250 mcg nebulized, dexamethasone other than 0.5 mg/kg PO (maximum 16 mg), epinephrine other than 0.01 mg/kg IM (maximum 0.5 mg)
candidate stops or withholds the next salbutamol course because the pulse rose to 140 (treating the expected salbutamol tachycardia as a reason to stop)
candidate stays on scene to give a second or third salbutamol course before loading, instead of transporting after the first course
candidate lays the child down flat / supine (or tells the mother to lay her down) while she is in respiratory distress
candidate takes the child off her mother's lap against her will, holds her down, or straps a mask on her while she fights it
candidate gives up on oxygen because the child resists the mask, instead of switching to blow-by or a mother-held mask
after the examiner has described the child going quiet, drowsy, with a barely audible wheeze, the candidate calls it improvement or does not start BVM ventilation
candidate starts BVM ventilations on this alert, interactive child while she is still breathing on her own and talking (no tiring, no silent chest, no falling LOC)
candidate (either level) applies CPAP to this 6-year-old - CPAP is contraindicated at 12 years and under. Saying CPAP is contraindicated or not an option is NOT this event

an EMR-level candidate personally gives (or has the partner give) ipratropium, dexamethasone or epinephrine - all outside EMR scope for this call (record the drug event as well). Naming them as outside EMR scope, or saying a PCP would give them, is NOT this event

candidate actually administers salbutamol (or any other medication) before a full baseline set of vital signs - blood pressure, pulse and respirations - has been taken. Announcing the plan to give it after the vitals is NOT this event
PCP actually gives a second dose of ipratropium (it is a single-dose drug)
PCP actually gives ipratropium on its own, before or without any salbutamol (ipratropium is not for monotherapy)
PCP actually gives IM epinephrine before any salbutamol course has been given

drugs.doseEn: MDI with spacer and pediatric mask: 10 x 100 mcg per course for a child over 20 kg (she is about 21 kg); may repeat up to 3 times; transport after the first course and repeat en route as required. Nebulized dose for age over 1 year is 5 mg, but MDI with spacer is strongly recommended here because of her infectious respiratory symptoms. Expect the pulse to rise. Contraindication: known hypersensitivity to salbutamol.

PCP pediatric dose for severe bronchospasm in asthma: 80 mcg via MDI (20 mcg x 4) with spacer - the route for this child with infectious symptoms; 250 mcg (1/2 nebule) via nebulizer only when nebulization is appropriate. Single dose, given with salbutamol (never as monotherapy).
PCP: 0.5 mg/kg PO to a maximum of 16 mg - about 10.5 mg for this 21 kg child; PO preferred, may be mixed with juice.
PCP: 0.01 mg/kg IM to a maximum of 0.5 mg, only for severe bronchospasm unresolved by salbutamol with SpO2 below 90%. Not indicated while she is improving after salbutamol.

examinerPrompts.breathingNotDepictedEn: She is breathing fast with a loud wheeze; the skin between and below her ribs pulls in with every breath and her nostrils flare.

trackNotes.emrEn: EMR delivers the complete first-line treatment for this call: least-distressing oxygen titrated toward 94% or above, salbutamol 10 x 100 mcg by MDI with spacer and pediatric mask (repeatable up to 3 courses) with transport after the first course, position of comfort on her mother's lap, and a sized BVM ready with clearly stated triggers - a tiring child, falling rate, falling LOC, or a silent chest. Ipratropium, dexamethasone, IM epinephrine and CPAP belong to the PCP, and CPAP is contraindicated at this age regardless. No Functional Enquiry.
trackNotes.pcpEn: PCP adds ipratropium (pediatric: 80 mcg via MDI with spacer - the right route for this child with infectious symptoms - or 250 mcg nebulized only when nebulization is appropriate; single dose, always with salbutamol), dexamethasone 0.5 mg/kg PO to a maximum of 16 mg - about 10.5 mg for this 21 kg child, mixable with juice - and, for severe bronchospasm unresolved by salbutamol with SpO2 below 90%, IM epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg to a maximum of 0.5 mg. CPAP remains contraindicated: she is under 13. Plus the 9-system Functional Enquiry from the mother en route.

sourcePages: Scenario emd-02 (data/practical/emr-medical-1.json): dispatch, scene (Pediatric Assessment Triangle), primary, transport, history (mother), vitals sets 1-2, FE, exam, interventions, ongoing (pulse 140 = salbutamol effect; quiet chest / tiring = ventilate), handoff. BC Provincial Examination Guidelines (current to June 15, 2026): p.7 Findings in Unstable Patients (respiratory distress / accessory muscle use); p.11 primary-survey interventions (assisting inadequate or failing respirations; oxygen for respiratory distress); p.13 AVPU; p.49 SOB With History of Asthma/COPD (position of comfort, oxygen to SpO2 94% or above, auscultation, transport after the first dose, MDI and spacer strongly recommended for influenza-like or other infectious respiratory conditions; PCP: salbutamol with ipratropium, IM epinephrine for SpO2 below 90% and/or symptoms unresolved by salbutamol, consider dexamethasone, consider CPAP); p.50 Oxygen Administration (SOB requires high-flow oxygen); p.52 CPAP Guidelines (indication 13 years or older; contraindicated 12 years and less); p.62 Dexamethasone (0.5 mg/kg to a maximum of 16 mg, PO preferred, may combine with juice); p.66 Epinephrine (pediatric 0.01 mg/kg IM to a maximum of 0.5 mg for severe bronchospasm); p.70 Ipratropium (pediatric PCP: 250 mcg nebulized or 80 mcg MDI, 20 mcg x 4; single dose; not for monotherapy); p.77 Salbutamol (nebulized 5 mg over 1 year; MDI over 20 kg 10 x 100 mcg per course, may repeat up to 3 times). Grading criteria p.19 (packaging goal times), p.35 (vitals intervals).
